text: Time to combine everything from this chapter into one concrete number. This lab walks through a small, illustrative three-gate circuit and computes an actual total error probability by combining decoherence and depolarizing noise — exactly the back-of-envelope calculation that justifies why error correction is necessary before you've written a single line of a correction code.

Consider three gates running sequentially on one qubit, on hardware with an illustrative T1 of 100 microseconds and a fixed depolarizing gate-error probability of 0.001 per gate. Gate 1 takes 20 nanoseconds, gate 2 takes 50, gate 3 takes 200 — different durations, so different decoherence risk. Each gate can go wrong two independent ways: it can decohere while executing, time-dependent from Lesson 1, or it can suffer a depolarizing gate error, roughly time-independent from Lessons 3 and 4. Treating these as independent, the probability a gate survives both is the product of each source's survival probability.

Working this out gate by gate: gate 1's decoherence is about 1.9998 times ten to the minus 4, plus a depolarizing probability of 0.001, giving a combined error of about 1.1998 times ten to the minus 3, or survival of 0.998800. Gate 2 combines to about 1.4994 times ten to the minus 3, survival 0.998501. Gate 3 combines to about 2.9960 times ten to the minus 3, survival 0.997004. Notice gate 3's combined error is almost exactly the sum of its two parts — the correction term, their product, is negligible at this scale.

The circuit survives cleanly only if all three gates individually survive, so the overall survival probability is the product of the three: 0.998800 times 0.998501 times 0.997004, which comes out to about 0.994315. That means the probability that at least one error occurred somewhere across the three gates is 1 minus 0.994315, about 5.6853 times ten to the minus 3 — roughly 0.57%.

A 0.57% chance of an error across just three gates might not sound alarming — but notice how fast this compounds. This tiny circuit already has a worse-than-one-in-200 chance of carrying at least one error. Scale the same illustrative rate up to a real algorithm's circuit, hundreds or thousands of gates deep, and the probability of zero errors anywhere collapses toward zero. Every number here is explicitly illustrative, not a measurement from any specific processor — the value of this exercise is the method, breaking a circuit into gates and composing their error probabilities, not the exact digits.

That's the unavoidable fact motivating the rest of this course: raw physical qubits cannot run a long computation error-free on their own. Next, Chapter 2 starts from classical error correction — the repetition code — before showing exactly why it doesn't port directly to the quantum setting.
